title: 200 core words
tomorrow: why would one verse say 'self' again and again?

segments.voice: Last week the 200 core words came back as a round: asmi, mamakah, iti, karma, bhu, sukha, datta. Now a root put to the test, and the words that tell you who's in a line.

A word never met before: nasam. Can a known root crack it? Split it: na, not, and asam. Asam leans on as, to be, the root under asmi. I was. So nasam: I was not. The guess holds. Now the scene where that word is said, already under way. A chariot stands between two armies. Arjuna has put down his bow, told his friend Krishna that he will not fight, and gone silent. The text says Krishna answers him as if smiling. And a few lines into that answer comes a sentence built almost entirely from the smallest words a reader can learn.
screen: `NASAM: A WORD NEVER MET.` → `NA + ASAM: I WAS NOT.` → `KRISHNA ANSWERS, AS IF SMILING.`

segments.voice: Here's the first half, Bhagavad Gita 2.12: na tv evaham jatu nasam, na tvam neme janadhipah. Open it with last week's tools. Evaham is eva plus aham, and aham is I. Nasam, already cracked: I was not. Neme is na plus ime: not these. So: never was I not, nor you, nor these lords of men. Tvam, you. Ime, these: the kings standing across the field. Then the second half: na chaiva na bhavishyamah sarve vayam atah param. Nor will we ever cease to be, all of us, from here on. Vayam, we. Sarve, all. Now watch the order the small words arrive in. I. You. These. Then we, all of us. Krishna starts with himself, adds his friend, adds the very people Arjuna can't bear to fight, and closes the circle into one word. The Gita spends many verses opening what that sentence means, and readers take it in different ways. For a reader of Sanskrit, the plain point lands first. Words like aham, tvam, ime and vayam come back again and again in these texts. Once they're known, a verse stops being a wall and becomes a room with people in it: who's speaking, who's being spoken to, and who's being pointed at across the field.
screen: `AHAM: I.` · `TVAM: YOU.` · `IME: THESE, ACROSS THE FIELD.` · `VAYAM: WE, ALL OF US.` · then, large: `A ROOM WITH PEOPLE IN IT.`

segments.voice: Say four small words out loud, slowly, one to a breath: aham, I; tvam, you; ime, these; vayam, we. On aham, feel your own breath; on tvam, bring one person to mind; on ime, the people around you today; on vayam, all of you together. Then let the words go and keep breathing.
Two hundred core words, and four of them today: aham, I; tvam, you; ime, these; vayam, we. The small words that tell a reader who's in the room.
Your line: 200 core words. Learn who's speaking, and a verse fills with people. A new week, begun.

notes: This stretch follows days 1463-1466 (to be; karma and phala; ca, eva, na, iti; roots kri, bhu, gam). Days 1467-1470 (roots; sukha and duhkha; datta; a review round) were read before the final pass; day 1471's hook answers 1470's tomorrow line (guessing a word from a known root).

Shape story: the hook is the 2.9-2.10 scene; the teach reads 2.12 for its pronouns. The philosophical claim of 2.12 (the eternal self) is left to 'the Gita spends many verses opening what that sentence means'.
Grammar: aham, tvam (singular), ime (masc. nom. pl.), vayam (1st pl.), asam (imperfect 1st sg. of as); confirm the plain-words descriptions.

Sanskrit is given in a simple romanization in the spoken text (no diacritics) so the voice can read it; the sources hold the same romanization. Confirm every word against a standard edition, and the verse numbers (editions differ by a verse around 1.27-1.28).
Grammar is described in plain words (endings, 'having done it', 'while doing it'); a Sanskritist should confirm each description.

Priya practices, ends up seated between them, recites with shaking hands, and the two men only stand near each other afterward (no overnight repair).
